title: Black gets the bishop out first
intro:
Black plays ...Bf5 or ...Bg4 before ...e6, so the bishop that is normally stuck behind the pawn wall gets out first. It is the sensible thing to do and it is the reason a Colle player has to know this chapter: the bishop that would have been Black's problem is now a piece.

## What changes

Not the setup. b3, Bb2, castle, knight to d2: all of it still happens. What changes is where White's own light-squared bishop belongs, and the answer depends on which square Black chose.

Against ...Bf5 the bishops stare at each other on the b1-h7 diagonal, so put yours on d3 and offer the trade. Black either takes, which develops your queen for nothing, or allows Bxf5, which leaves Black with doubled f-pawns and a permanent weakness on e6 and h7.

There is a trap in that offer, and it is worth a piece. Until Black has a pawn on e6 or g6, NOTHING recaptures on f5. So after 3...Bf5 4.Bd3, a natural move like 4...c6 simply loses the bishop to 5.Bxf5. Look at the recapture before you assume a trade is a trade.

Against ...Bg4 the bishop is not on your diagonal at all, it is pinning your knight. Ask it the question with h3. If Black takes on f3, recapture with the QUEEN, never with the pawn: the queen lands on f3 pointing at b7 and d5, which is exactly where the bishop on b2 will be pointing too. If Black keeps the pin with ...Bh5, put your own bishop on e2, break the pin, and carry on as usual.

## The one thing worth memorising

Recapture on f3 with the queen. Recapture on d3 with the queen. In both cases the queen comes to a good square with a free move, and in both cases the pawn recapture would wreck a structure you spent the whole opening building.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Taking on f3 with the g-pawn and opening your own king. Playing h3 and then g4 without a reason, which weakens the squares your knight wants. Leaving the bishop on d3 when Black's bishop has gone to g4, where it is doing nothing. And forgetting that after Bxf5 exf5 the pawn on f5 is a target, not a strength.

Break the pin by blocking it. The bishop is a little passive on e2 and it is doing the one job that matters.

tree.note: Black hits d4 before the bishop on c8 has decided: the Slav course's move against this setup, played before ...e6 so that the bishop keeps its diagonal.

children.note: The bishop to its square, as always. The engine would rather 4.c4, and the Zukertort player keeps the setup: the bishop first, and the pawn to b3 or c4 once the knight on b8 has said where it is going.

mistakes.note: The Colle proper, holding d4 with the pawn. Sound, and it is the other course: this one puts the bishop out and the pawn on b3.
Sound: 4...e6 5.a3 Bxc5 6.b4 and the pawn is kept for a while. It gives Black the centre for it.
The setup a move too early: 4...Nc6 5.Bb2 cxd4 6.exd4 Bg4 and the bishop on f1 is still at home with the centre open.

children.note: Development, with a second attacker on d4.
Castle first. With the knight on c6 hitting d4, b3 at once lets ...cxd4 open the centre before the king is safe; castled, the setup follows with b3 and Bb2, or c4 if Black takes on d4.

mistakes.note: 5...cxd4 6.exd4 Bg4 and the centre has opened with the king still on e1 and the bishop on c1 not yet on b2.
Sound and the Colle proper. Castling keeps the choice of b3 or c4.
5...cxd4 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.exd4 Bg4 and the knight has been traded for a knight that was doing nothing, with the pawn on c6 holding d5.

children.plan: b3 and Bb2 when ...e6 has shut the bishop on c8 in, c4 when Black takes on d4 first. The position is level and the structure is the one the course teaches; the difference from the main line is only that the bishop on c8 is still free, so Bb2 waits for ...e6.
